paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: Boyle's law describes how the pressure and the volume of a gas are tied together. Take a fixed amount of gas, seal it in, and hold its temperature steady. Its pressure and volume are then inversely proportional: when one goes up, the other goes down. Put another way, pressure multiplied by volume stays the same number as long as the temperature does not change.

paragraphs.heading: The equation
paragraphs.text: In symbols the law reads PV = k. Here P is the pressure, V is the volume, and k is a constant set by the temperature and the amount of gas. To compare one sample in two situations, it is written P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, where P₁ and V₁ are the starting pressure and volume and P₂ and V₂ are the new ones. This lets you predict how one quantity changes when you change the other, provided the gas ends at the same temperature it started at.

paragraphs.heading: A quick example
paragraphs.text: Squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles. Let it spread into twice the space and its pressure drops to half. When the pressure on a gas rises, its volume falls because the particles of gas are pushed closer together.

paragraphs.heading: Boyle's J-shaped tube
paragraphs.text: Richard Towneley and Henry Power first noticed the link between pressure and volume in the 17th century. Robert Boyle then confirmed it by experiment and published the law in 1662. He trapped air in the closed end of a J-shaped tube and poured mercury in at the other end, so the mercury pressed on the air and made it shrink. Repeating this with different amounts of mercury, he found that pressure and volume were inversely proportional. Some authorities say his assistant, Robert Hooke, built the apparatus.

paragraphs.heading: Mariotte's version
paragraphs.text: The French physicist Edme Mariotte found the same law on his own in 1679, after Boyle had already published it in 1662. Mariotte also discovered that the volume of air changes with temperature. That is why the rule is sometimes called Mariotte's law or the Boyle–Mariotte law. It was the first physical law written as an equation showing how two changing quantities depend on each other.

paragraphs.heading: Where it breaks down
paragraphs.text: At middling pressures and temperatures, most gases act like ideal gases. In the 17th century, equipment could not reach very high pressures or very low temperatures, so departures from the law were unlikely to show up. As technology reached those extremes, gases were seen to stray from ideal behaviour, and only real gas theory describes their pressure and volume accurately. The size of the departure is expressed through a quantity called the compressibility factor.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining it with particles
paragraphs.text: Boyle and Mariotte reached the law purely through experiment. It can also be worked out in theory by assuming a gas is made of atoms and molecules in motion whose collisions are perfectly elastic, which is the basis of the kinetic theory of gases. Daniel Bernoulli did this in 1737–1738 by applying Newton's laws of motion to molecules. At the time, many scientists strongly resisted these assumptions, seeing them as pure theory with no observational evidence behind them.
